newsitem.title: THAILAND: Chesterton Thai appointed Somprasong valuer.
newsitem.headline: Chesterton Thai appointed Somprasong valuer.

text.p: Preliminary independent assessment of troubled Thai developer Somprasong Land Plc has begun with the hiring of Chesterton Thai Ltd to value Somprasong's properties, executives said.

Somprasong, a medium-sized property developer, last week became the first Thai company to default on a Eurobond, when it failed to honour a $3.1 million interest payment due on its $80 million Euroconvertible issue.

The default sent shudders through a Thai bourse already trading at over four and a half year lows, and raised fears about the financial stability of some other Thai developers caught by a slump in the Thai property market.
"I can confirm that we have been instructed to perform a valuation on Somprasong's property," said Jeremy Bradbeer, managing director of Chesterton Thai.
"Discussions went through several interested parties before we were contacted. The signing of a contract is imminent ... as far as we are concerned the process is underway," Bradbeer said.

Somprasong last week issued a statement to the Stock Exchange of Thailand which said a valuation of its assets will be completed by 21 March. Initial talks with creditors are set to begin on 24 March.

The firm's secured creditors, which include a number of large local banks and finance houses, are trying to reach a concensus on the handling of Somprasong, executives said. The Eurobond holders are unsecured.
"The secured creditors are trying to come up with a common position from which negotiations with unsecured creditors can begin," a senior Somprasong advisor told Reuters.
The secured creditors include Siam Commercial Bank Plc and Bangkok Bank Plc, and finance companies National Finance and Securities Plc and Ekachart Finance and Securities Plc.

Siam Commercial Bank, which was asked by the central bank to assist Somprasong, said initial reaction from other creditors to transfer select Somprasong assets and liabilities to a new company had been largely positive.

"It is at a very preliminary stage ... but it seems it would be clumsy taking over the company and it easier to form a new company. My guess is that creditors will probably co-operate to participate in the equity of a new company and an operator would be brought in to run it, but don't expect anything soon" said a senior executive.
"Those who may not wish to join can still work it out legally with the existing company," he said.
